subject: Vocabulary
topic: One-Word Substitution — Advanced Set II (W11 B2)

questions.stem: One who can use both hands with equal ease:
questions.explanation: B is correct. AMBIDEXTROUS = able to use both hands equally well. Etymology: ambi (both) + dexter (right hand in Latin) → originally 'having two right hands'. Trap: Ambiguous = having two possible meanings (ambi+agere); Ambivalent = having mixed feelings (ambi+valent=strong); Amphibious = living in both water and land. All start with 'ambi' (both) but refer to different domains.

questions.stem: A person who pretends to be what they are not, especially in matters of morality:
questions.explanation: C is correct. HYPOCRITE = a person who says or claims to have higher moral standards or beliefs than actually possessed; one who pretends to be virtuous but acts otherwise. Etymology: Greek 'hypokrites' = actor. Trap: Charlatan = a person falsely claiming expertise/skill (mainly professional fraud); Demagogue = a political leader appealing to prejudices; Misanthrope = someone who dislikes and avoids people.

questions.stem: The study and collection of postage stamps:
questions.explanation: C is correct. PHILATELY = the collection and study of postage stamps and postal history. Etymology: Greek 'philos' (loving) + 'ateles' (exempt from tax) — stamps showed postage was paid. Trap: Philharmonic = loving music (phil+harmonia); Philology = study of languages (phil+logos); Philanthropy = love of humanity (phil+anthropos). All share the 'phil' (love) root but study/love different things.

questions.stem: Words written on a tomb or gravestone:
questions.explanation: B is correct. EPITAPH = an inscription on a tombstone or a short text honouring a dead person. Etymology: Greek 'epi' (upon) + 'taphos' (tomb). Trap: Epitome = a person or thing that is a perfect example of a quality (not a tomb inscription); Epigraph = an inscription on a building or a short quotation at the start of a book; Epigram = a short witty poem or saying. The 'epi' prefix means 'upon' in all cases, but the root changes the meaning.

questions.stem: A person who is indifferent to both pleasure and pain:
questions.explanation: B is correct. STOIC = a person who endures pain or hardship without showing feelings or complaining; indifferent to pleasure and pain. From the Stoic school of philosophy (Stoicism). Trap: Epicurean = devoted to pleasure and luxury (from Epicurus' philosophy of pleasure); Hedonist = one who pursues pleasure as the highest good; Ascetic = one who practices severe self-discipline and abstains from pleasure (an ascetic avoids pleasure but is not indifferent — they actively abstain). Stoic specifically implies emotional indifference to both.

questions.stem: An office or post that provides an income but requires little or no work:
questions.explanation: A is correct. SINECURE = a position requiring little or no work yet providing a salary or income. Etymology: Latin 'sine cura' = without care/concern. Historically, church positions 'without the care of souls' that still paid. Trap: Tenure = the period of holding a position (not necessarily easy); Stipend = a regular fixed payment (a type of income, not the job itself); Perquisite = a benefit beyond salary (a perk). Sinecure specifically describes the position/office itself as undemanding.

questions.stem: The practice of having more than one wife or husband at the same time:
questions.explanation: A is correct. POLYGAMY = the practice of having multiple spouses simultaneously (can be multiple wives OR multiple husbands). Etymology: poly (many) + gamos (marriage). Trap: Polyandry = specifically a woman having multiple husbands (poly+andros=man); Polygyny = specifically a man having multiple wives (poly+gyne=woman); Bigamy = the crime of marrying someone while already married to another (illegal in most countries; implies exactly 2 marriages). Polygamy is the broadest term covering all multiple-spouse arrangements.

C is correct. MISOGAMIST = a person who hates or dislikes marriage. Etymology: miso (hatred) + gamos (marriage). Trap: Misanthrope = a person who hates human beings in general (miso+anthropos); Misogynist = a person who hates or has prejudice against women (miso+gyne); Celibate = a person who deliberately abstains from marriage and often from sexual activity (not from hatred but from choice, often religious). Misogamist is the specific one-word substitute for 'hater of marriage'.

questions.stem: A statement that seems self-contradictory but actually contains some truth:
questions.explanation: B is correct. PARADOX = a seemingly absurd or self-contradictory statement or proposition that when investigated or explained proves to be well-founded or true. Example: 'Less is more.' Trap: Oxymoron = a figure of speech where contradictory terms are combined ('deafening silence', 'living death') — the contradiction is intentional and within a phrase; Tautology = saying the same thing twice in different words ('free gift'); Euphemism = a mild word substituted for a harsh one ('passed away' for 'died'). A paradox is the broader statement-level seeming contradiction that resolves to truth.

questions.stem: A government run by the wealthiest members of society:
questions.explanation: C is correct. PLUTOCRACY = a society or system governed by the wealthy. Etymology: Greek 'ploutos' (wealth) + 'kratos' (rule). Trap: Oligarchy = rule by a small group of people (not necessarily wealthy; oligos=few); Aristocracy = rule by the nobility or privileged class (not specifically the wealthiest, but the 'best-born'; aristos=best); Theocracy = rule by religious authorities (theos=god). Confusables: plutocracy (wealth), aristocracy (nobility), oligarchy (few), theocracy (religion), democracy (people), autocracy (one person).
